title: Pre-race determinants influencing performance and finishing of a transcontinental 4486-km ultramarathon
authors: Schutz UH, Ehrhardt M, Beer M, Schmidt-Trucksass A, Billich C
journal: The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness
population: Participants of the TransEurope FootRace 2009 (4,486 km in 64 stages, average 70.1 km/day)
findings: 71% of the 44 analysed participants finished; mean running speed was 8.25 km/h; mean pre-race training volume exceeded 5,500 km (the abstract says the mean volume 'extends 5500 km', stated for the last year).
Finishers and non-finishers did not differ significantly in any tested pre-race determinant.
There was no association between years of regular running, number of finished marathons, ultramarathons or multistage ultramarathons and race performance.
Pre-race training intensity (km/h) correlated very strongly and positively with race performance; training volume correlated with a medium effect size.
Pre-race records in 6-hour, 50-km and 100-km races correlated highly with race performance; ultra performance correlated inversely with age.
limitations: Only 44 runners in one extreme multi-stage event; low power to detect finisher vs non-finisher differences; self-reported training; not generalisable to 200-mile single-stage races.
implications: For multi-day and stage events, estimate goal pace from recent 50 to 100 km race performance and last-year training speed, not volume alone.
Do not promise that high pre-race volume prevents dropout in multi-stage events: no pre-race variable separated finishers from non-finishers, so in-event management should carry risk guidance.
No numeric volume target for multi-stage events is justified; show 5,500 km/year only as a descriptive reference for an experienced field.

verification.notes: Crossref (2019-11, first author Schutz with umlaut) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched. Added the stated null associations for running history that the researcher omitted.
